prompts.L1:

With her one horrid eye persistently unfastened, a vigilant bird watched my grandfather during the Great Depression use each evening of one whole year to wander his corn fields knowing this world is just one pig after another in one pen after another. Therefore, the bird heard him suppose, shouldn’t he with his best gun, machete, Buick, or rope terminate his acquaintance with the tiresome setup of breakfast-lunch-dinner-dawn-dusk-fall-winter-spring-summer- blah-blah-blah? But his girls were good-looking and made such fine pies, so the bird watched him live wretchedly until he died more naturally of cancer too soon to see his people become the dopefiends, doctor-haters, masturbators, insomniacs, sleep fanatics, shut-ins, and teetotalers the bird knew they would become, for the purpose of girls is to just ruin everything with wanton reproduction so that now now now it’s really relentless—how heavy his people got in their limbs and how torrential, thus, the frenzied wind, though beyond the eye of the bird is the small, ashen brain of the bird, and below that, a heart, I swear, through which come the iffy notes of this cruel song.

And so, the bird heard him wonder: should he not, with his best gun, his machete, his Buick, or a rope, terminate his acquaintance with the tiresome arrangement of breakfast-lunch-dinner, dawn-dusk, fall-winter-spring-summer—blah-blah-blah? For the purpose of girls is simply to ruin everything through wanton reproduction, so that now, now, now, it is truly relentless: how heavy his people have grown in their limbs, and how torrential, therefore, the frenzied wind. Yet beyond the bird’s eye lies the small, ashen brain of the bird, and below that, a heart, I swear, through which pass the uncertain notes of this cruel song.
outputs.L2: A watchful bird, one awful eye always stuck open, observed my grandfather in the Great Depression as he spent every evening for an entire year roaming through his cornfields, aware that life was nothing but pig after pig in pen after pen. And so, the bird heard him wonder whether he ought to use his finest gun, a machete, his Buick, or a length of rope to end his involvement with the exhausting routine of breakfast, lunch, dinner, dawn, dusk, autumn, winter, spring, summer, and all the rest of it. Yet his daughters were beautiful and baked excellent pies, and so the bird saw him go on living miserably until he died, in a more ordinary way, of cancer—too early to watch his descendants become the addicts, enemies of doctors, masturbators, insomniacs, sleep-obsessives, recluses, and abstainers from alcohol that the bird already understood they would turn into. After all, the role of girls is simply to spoil everything through reckless reproduction, so that now, now, now the burden has become truly unceasing: how ponderous his people grew in their bodies, and how violently, because of that, the crazed wind poured down. Yet behind the bird’s eye lies its small gray brain, and beneath that a heart, I insist, and through that heart drift the uncertain tones of this merciless song.
outputs.L3:
A vigilant bird watched from above as the narrator’s grandfather moved through the difficult years of the Great Depression. From its perch, it saw him walking the fields, burdened by poverty, failure, and despair. The cornfields that should have promised nourishment and survival instead became a place of exhaustion and hopeless reflection. As he wandered among the rows, the grandfather felt trapped in the sameness of his life: planting, harvesting, struggling, and beginning again, with little reward and no clear escape.

In those moments, he contemplated suicide. The weight of his circumstances pressed heavily on him, and the repetitive labor of farm life seemed to mirror the bleak repetition of existence itself. Life appeared to him as a cycle of suffering, work, disappointment, and decay. Yet even in his deepest misery, he was held back by his love for his daughters. The thought of them, and of the small domestic comforts they shared, gave him a reason to continue. Their presence—ordinary, tender, and familiar—kept him attached to life when despair might otherwise have overcome him.

The grandfather eventually died of cancer, and in a grim sense, his death spared him from witnessing the later troubles of his descendants. He did not live to see the dysfunction, pain, and emotional damage that would unfold in the generations after him. The family’s suffering did not end with his hardships; it continued in new forms, passed down through time.

The bird’s perspective gives this story a cold, watchful distance. It observes human anguish not as an isolated tragedy, but as part of a larger and more merciless pattern. From the bird’s view, the grandfather’s despair, his daughters’ lives, and the later struggles of the family all belong to the same relentless cycle of survival, reproduction, suffering, and death. The natural world continues without pity, and human beings, like all creatures, are caught within its cruel repetitions.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents a bleak family history shaped by Depression-era despair, suicidal ideation, and a sense of generational decline. At its center is the narrator’s grandfather, whose life appears marked less by heroic struggle than by exhaustion, poverty, and the grim persistence required simply to continue living. His suffering is not described in a straightforward realist manner alone; instead, it is filtered through the strange, surreal perspective of a one-eyed bird that watches him. This watchful bird gives the scene an uncanny quality, as though human misery is being observed from outside ordinary human sympathy. Its single eye suggests a distorted but penetrating vision, one that sees the grandfather not as an isolated individual but as part of a larger pattern of pain.

Through this perspective, the grandfather’s despair becomes more than a private crisis. His suicidal thoughts and emotional collapse reflect the pressures of an era in which economic hardship reduced life to endurance. Yet the passage also implies that endurance itself is not necessarily redemptive. To survive, marry, work, and reproduce may seem like ordinary human achievements, but here these acts are presented as mechanisms by which suffering is passed forward. The family continues, but continuity does not bring renewal; it carries misery into the next generation.

In this sense, the “cruel song” takes on a darkly comic yet tragic meaning. A song is usually associated with beauty, expression, or celebration, but this one is cruel because it sings of repetition, instinct, and inherited pain. The bird’s presence makes the family’s suffering seem both absurd and inevitable, as if human beings are trapped in a natural cycle they cannot fully understand or escape. The result is a vision of life in which reproduction and ordinary perseverance do not defeat despair but extend it. The passage therefore transforms a family story into a grim meditation on inherited human misery, suggesting that what is passed down through generations is not only blood or memory, but also anguish.
outputs.L5:
With the onset of the Great Depression, millions of people around the world faced unemployment, poverty, and uncertainty. The economic crisis, which began in 1929, affected families, businesses, and entire nations. Banks failed, factories closed, and many people struggled to afford basic necessities such as food and shelter.

Despite these hardships, the Great Depression also showed the resilience of communities. People helped one another, shared resources, and looked for new ways to survive. Governments began to take a larger role in supporting citizens and rebuilding economies. In the United States, programs introduced during the New Deal aimed to create jobs, provide relief, and restore confidence.

The Great Depression remains an important historical lesson. It reminds us that economic systems can be fragile, but it also shows that with determination, cooperation, and effective leadership, societies can recover from even the most difficult times.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single long, bleakly comic literary paragraph about a one-eyed bird watching a grandfather in the Great Depression contemplate suicide in his cornfields, with repetitions, dark family prophecy, and an absurd fatalistic tone.
counterfactuals.output: The one-eyed bird, who had lost the other eye in some private avian calamity and had therefore acquired the permanent expression of a judge who has already read the verdict and found the defendant tiresome, sat on the split fencepost at the edge of the cornfield and watched Grandfather stand among the stalks in the summer of the Great Depression, that national season of empty pockets, cracked plates, thin soup, thinner prayers, and men staring into distances as if distances might finally have the decency to answer; watched him with its one black bead of sight while the corn, mean and stunted and yellowing at the tips, rattled around him like a crowd whispering the same bad news in a thousand dry tongues, watched him take off his hat, put it on again, take it off, put it on again, as if the ceremony of despair required a costume change, watched him look toward the house where Grandmother was boiling nothing into something and the children were learning the family arithmetic—one potato divided by seven mouths equals God’s mysterious will—and watched him look toward the sky, which was blank, and toward the barn, which leaned, and toward his hands, which were honest and useless, and the bird blinked its only eye as if to say, Yes, yes, here we are again, the old bargain, the old joke, a man and his land both failing to produce. In our family it was later said, and said often, and then said even more often because misfortune becomes respectable when repeated at supper, that the bird had been expected, that some great-aunt with hair like smoke and a Bible full of pressed weeds had once prophesied a one-eyed bird would come to watch the men of our bloodline at the hour when they mistook themselves for the end of the story; she had said, “When the cyclops bird sits west of the corn and the corn speaks like bones in a bucket, a son of this house will consider returning himself unopened to the Lord,” which was a queer thing to say at a baptism and caused several cousins to drop their cake, but history, like a drunk mule, has a way of backing into the very gate it was warned about. So there was Grandfather, unopened or over-opened, depending on whom you ask, standing in his defeated field with the bank at his back and hunger in the house and the dust of Oklahoma or Kansas or Nebraska or whichever biblical punishment the county assessor preferred that year sneaking into his collar, and there was the bird, black or brown or the color of old coffee, depending on which uncle had been drinking when he told it, cocking its head, cocking its terrible little head, as if urging him to make up his mind because it had other appointments with other doomed men along other rows of corn, and all around them the farm performed its comic opera of collapse: the scarecrow wore Grandfather’s better shirt and still had more stuffing than the children, the pig had developed the delicate moral superiority of an animal too poor to slaughter, the mule refused to move except in the direction of bankruptcy, and the windmill turned and turned without pumping anything, a perfect machine for illustrating the family. Grandfather, who had believed in work the way some men believe in angels, found work standing beside him now like a large embarrassed angel with no wings and mud on its boots, saying nothing useful, and he thought of his father, who had died owing money, and his father’s father, who had died owing apologies, and his father’s father’s father, who had supposedly been chased from a county in Tennessee by a widow with a skillet and a legal claim, and he understood, with the clear calm of a man who has finally added the figures correctly, that the family prophecy was not a warning but an inventory: one blind hope, one bad harvest, one bird, one man in a field, repeat, repeat, repeat. The bird scratched itself. This was perhaps the cruelest part. While Grandfather weighed the enormous philosophical question of whether a man could step out of his own life without leaving muddy tracks on the kitchen floor of eternity, the bird scratched under its wing with bureaucratic indifference, then fluffed itself into a ragged ball, then released a small white punctuation mark onto the fencepost, as if signing the scene on behalf of fate. And because our family has never been granted tragedy without slapstick, Grandfather began to laugh—not merrily, not sanely, not in any way that would have reassured the Methodist minister, but with the dry hiccuping laugh of a man who realizes the universe has hired poultry as its notary—and the corn rattled, and the bird stared, and the house waited, and the children inside kept quiet because children in those days knew the sound of a father thinking too hard. He did not die that afternoon, which some call mercy and others call poor scheduling; he put his hat back on for the last time, cursed the bird, cursed the corn, cursed Herbert Hoover, cursed the Lord in a whisper because he was not yet ready to be impolite at full volume, and walked back toward the house with the solemn wobble of a condemned man reprieved by clerical error, while behind him the one-eyed bird lifted itself from the post and flapped away over the rows, ugly, official, immortal, leaving the field to its dust and the family to its inheritance: the certainty that doom was coming, the stronger certainty that it would be ridiculous, and the strongest certainty of all that when it arrived someone would be watching from a fencepost, missing an eye, understanding everything, and offering no help whatsoever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Faulkner/Vonnegut-style stream-of-consciousness passage narrated through or around a vigilant bird, involving a Depression-era farmer, his daughters, pies, cancer, future dysfunctional descendants, and the cruelty of ordinary life.
counterfactuals.output:
The bird watched from the black hinge of the barn roof, one foot drawn up like a miser’s fist, the other clamped to the tin hot from the noon sun, and if birds know hunger then it knew it in the bright, exact way a needle knows cloth. Below, in the yard, the farmer moved as if the earth had loaned him his bones at interest.

His name was Enoch Bale, though the bank called him Mr. Bale on paper and boy in person, and the drought called him nothing at all. It only opened its dry mouth over the corn and breathed. The year was one of those years when even the calendar seemed ashamed to turn its pages, the Depression sitting everywhere like a relative who had come to stay and had taken the best chair and the last biscuit.

Enoch had three daughters, all elbows and braids and bare feet hardened by the yard, and they carried pies from the kitchen window to the table set under the chinaberry tree: apple if you believed in memory, vinegar if you believed in arithmetic, and one made from green tomatoes because his wife, Lottie, had said a pie was not a fruit but an intention. Lottie was inside, lying still in the room where the curtains had been washed until they were almost more hole than cloth, with the cancer working at her in the dark industriously, like a tenant farmer of the flesh. Nobody said cancer at the table. They said tired. They said spell. They said the Lord’s will, which is what people call a thing when it has already happened and they cannot afford a doctor.

The bird tilted its head.

It saw the knife go down through the crust. It saw the eldest girl, Ruth, count the slices without moving her lips, already apprenticed to loss. It saw Maybelle slap Junie’s hand because Junie had touched the sugared rim before grace, and then Maybelle cried because the slap had sounded too much like their father. Enoch bowed his head and thanked God for bounty, though bounty had not been properly introduced to that farm in years, and the bird, who had no theology except the worm and the hawk, dropped a white comma on the roof and waited.

So it goes, though nobody said that then either.

Years later—which are all already present if you are a bird, or a dying woman, or a child learning that love is a bowl passed around too small—Ruth would marry a man who smelled of machine oil and would keep her flour in coffee cans and her fear in her jaw. Maybelle would have a son who drank what his grandfather had swallowed silently, and that son would have a daughter who moved to a city of glass and elevators and paid a stranger to listen to the old farm speaking through her throat. Junie would leave home with a traveling salesman and come back twice, each time thinner, each time with a new laugh that fit poorly, like a dress borrowed for a funeral. Their children and their children’s children would inherit nothing visible from Enoch Bale: not land, not money, not even the Bible with the names in it, which would mildew in a trunk and be eaten along its begats. What they would inherit was the weather inside the house. The sudden silence after a plate broke. The conviction that sweetness must be earned by suffering. The habit of cutting pies into slices so narrow they looked like accusations.

And the bird watched that too, or another bird did, which is much the same thing.

Because there is always a bird somewhere, on a wire, a sill, a blasted fencepost, alert as a creditor, seeing the ordinary cruelty of things: the mule whipped not from malice but exhaustion; the girl told not now until her wanting curled back into her like a burned leaf; the mother turning her face to the wall so the children would not see her teeth clenched against the pain; the father standing in the field at dusk with his hat in his hands, hating the sky because it would not rain and hating himself because the hatred had nowhere useful to go.

When Lottie died, Enoch baked no pies. The girls did, because people came. People always come when there is a death, bringing food as if death were a rude guest that might be distracted by ham. They stood in the parlor and praised Lottie’s patience, which was only pain that had run out of witnesses. They said Enoch was taking it hard, which meant he had not wept where they could see. The bird landed on the windowsill and peered through the wavy glass at the shape under the sheet, the daughters in their washed dresses, the farmer’s hands hanging empty at his sides like tools after the work is finished and the barn has burned.

The youngest, Junie, saw the bird and almost smiled.

Then Enoch shut the window.

That was the whole history of the family, if you want the truth: something small and living appearing at the edge of grief, and a tired man shutting the window because he thought he was keeping out the flies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: For a year, my grandfather wandered the cornfields each night beneath the nail-paring moon, watched by the same black bird on the scarecrow’s shoulder, his mind circling guns and ropes, suppers gone cold, the turning seasons, bloodlines, births, and the damp, unharvestable sorrow of being alive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental literary monologue in one sprawling sentence that begins “With her one horrid eye…” and includes a bird, the Great Depression, a grandfather, suicide tools, daughters who bake pies, cancer, and a bitter meditation on descendants.
counterfactuals.output: With her one horrid eye, the bird saw everything: the Great Depression folded like a black handkerchief in my grandfather’s coat pocket, the rope and razor and pistol laid out not as invitations but as relics of a century’s exhausted vocabulary, the daughters who baked pies with crimped, obedient edges while cancer bloomed in the pantry of the body, and all the descendants arriving afterward like unpaid bills, bright-faced and ignorant, carrying our names forward as if inheritance were a blessing and not merely the stubborn migration of hunger, shame, and unfinished grief through blood that keeps congratulating itself for surviving
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly humorous, poetic paragraph in the style of contemporary American short fiction, where a bird observes an old farmer’s despair and the narrator digresses into family degeneration, bodily heaviness, wind, and the bird’s tiny heart singing a cruel song.
counterfactuals.output: The crow sat on the sagging fence post and watched the old farmer fold himself beside the empty trough, his hat in his hands like a dead animal he’d finally stopped pretending could be revived. All afternoon the wind had worried the fields down to their stubble, dragging dust through the yard and making the house groan in its joints, that house where three generations had learned the same poor arts: how to drink before noon, how to marry sorrow and call it weather, how to pass down bad teeth, bad knees, and the talent for sitting in a room until the room seemed to rot around you. The farmer’s body looked too heavy for the earth and not heavy enough for heaven, a sack of bones and gravy set down by mistake in a world increasingly committed to efficiency. His sons had gone soft in distant towns, his daughters hard in nearer ones; even the dog had taken to sleeping under the truck with the moral superiority of the employed. Above him, the crow puffed its black coat against the gale, bright-eyed and immaculate, and in its tiny furious heart there rose a song as thin as wire and twice as useful: poor man, poor meat, poor kingdom of mud—how sweetly everything ends when it ends for someone else.
